title: Traceability: how to find a batch’s journey in 20 minutes
excerpt: A complete answer to “Where did this batch come from?” should take 2–4 hours. See which journals connect the chain and how to run a quarterly traceability test.

body.text: Traceability is the ability to quickly reconstruct a product’s journey: from its supplier and invoice number to the specific dish served to a guest. An inspector is working against a timer: good practice is to provide a complete answer within 2–4 hours.

Once a quarter, a manager or technologist runs an exercise: they choose a random batch, and the team must assemble the chain backward (supplier → transport → receipt → storage → processing → serving) and forward (where the product went and which dishes were prepared) within the allotted time.

items: Goods-receipt journal with the invoice number.
Incoming-inspection journal linked to the batch.
Kitchen labeling (when the package was opened and when the product was processed).
Product-inspection journal for the prepared dish.
Receipts or cash-register sales data for the period.

body.title: What electronic records provide
body.text: The batch number from an invoice is automatically added to all related journals. Searching by batch takes seconds instead of flipping through a paper folder.
Why this matters to a business

Beyond inspections, traceability protects your reputation. If your dish is blamed for a food-poisoning incident, good traceability can either clear your kitchen of suspicion or give you grounds to make a claim against the supplier.
